en: Salutations to Śrī Śiva.
The Illuminator of the Meaning of the Distinctions.
[The Method for the Instruction on Brahman in the First Section] Homage to Śrī Śiva! Homage to the venerable Someśa-liṅga of Aṭṭapura, who exists in the form of the liṅga.
Salutations to you, whose own form is the unity of the Linga and the body; salutations to you, the embodiment of the Linga.
The word "namaḥ" is Umā herself; the word "śiva" is Śiva himself.
The letter 'a' and the sound 'ya'—their union is Soma; him we worship. || 2 ||
Śiva is the Liṅga and Umā is the body; thus, he is joined with her.
We worship these three words: "Soma," "Saṃbandha," and "Iti. || 3 ||
Henceforth, I shall proclaim that which illuminates the specific meaning.
The dialogue between the teacher and the disciple as declared in the Śivasiddhāntatantra.
Therein, first, the procedure for the instruction on Brahman in its six aspects is stated.
In the second [chapter], the correct procedure for the worship of the Śiva-liṅga is fully described. || 5 ||
The true nature of the glorious grace is proclaimed in the third [chapter].
In the fourth [chapter], the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for the six locations of Brahman is prescribed (or: is explained).
That which is proclaimed as the fifth is the rule for the conclusion.
Thus, the fivefold basis illuminates the specific meaning. || 7 ||
This [teaching], arising from the Sūtra on the Experience of Śiva, is now described in its proper sequence.
May the virtuous ones who experience Śiva rejoice eternally upon hearing this. || 8 ||
The Definition of the Guru
The Guru.
Now, therefore, [I shall explain] the supreme method of instruction known as the Sixfold Abode of Brahman (Ṣaṭsthalabrahma).
I shall explain in detail that which is born from the Śivasiddhāntatantra.
Just as it was previously taught and spoken by Ṣaṭsthalabrahmaśambhu.
The meaning taught to the Six-faced One is likewise stated here now.
(The purification of the six paths is taught therein: For the sake of purifying the six paths, the Śāmbhava Brahman of the six stations has been proclaimed.
The instruction consists of the six paths, beginning with the path of mantras, in their proper sequence.
The path of mantra, the path of words, and the path of phonemes—thus [they are distinguished] according to sound.
The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), and the path of the limited powers (kalādhvan) are recorded as such.
Having performed everything at the proper time, according to one's ability, and in accordance with the prescribed rules.
One who desires [success] there should perform what is appropriate with devotion. || 13 ||
Having raised up the five mudrās, provided with five corners.
Pervaded by five digits (kalās) and likewise consisting of the five powers (śaktis).
Outside, one should draw a maṇḍala with rice grains of five colors or even a single color.
Outside of that, however, is a square, by way of the form of the sacrificial strewing.
That auspicious lotus, complete with a pericarp, is encircled by a ring. || 15 ||
In the center of that, one should contemplate Śiva, who is directly the Praṇava and consists of the five Brahmans.
In each of the five pentagons, [place] the five syllables in sequence.
The five [faces] beginning with Sadyojāta consist of the letters starting from 'na' and ending with 'ya'.
By whom the five principles were entirely sealed with the five [mudrās]. || 17 ||
That is declared to be the Mudrā; it is the Śāmbhavī known as the Pañcamudrā.
This is the five great mudrās, declared to be the Śiva-yantra. || 18 ||
There, according to the prescribed rite and accompanied by mantras, he [placed] vessels that were pure, full, and very beautiful.
[He taught] the six stages consisting of conduct, the liṅga, devotion, the limbs, and so forth.
Taking up six water-pots, one should indeed place five in the five corners.
Having established one in the center, one should then proceed in sequence according to the prescribed rule.
Having surrounded the jars, beginning with the Praṇava, with pure threads.
Having placed kuśa grass, dūrvā grass, and mango sprouts into each of their mouths.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, together with the mantras, in the proper sequence.
Then, having praised and bowed down to these six in their proper sequence, || 22 ||
Facing north, the Guru should cause the disciple to face west and restrain him.
Then, having performed the consecration with the auspicious waters contained in the jars, [he should proceed].
Having then performed the descent of power (śaktipāta) for the sake of the full increase of right knowledge.
For those embodied beings upon whom [his] power falls, there is no turning back.
Their characteristic mark is an eagerness for liberation and an aversion to remaining in worldly existence.
Devotion toward the devotees of Śiva, and faith in the ritual prescribed by his teaching. (25)
The glorious five-syllabled mantra, together with the *tāra*, is indeed the six-syllabled one.
It is endowed with the six-limbed Liṅga and possesses the splendor of Brahman in its six stations.
Then, having fully instructed him in the Śivasiddhāntatantra along with its essential meaning, [he said:]
Whatever is stated in this Śivānubhavasūtra, that one should teach.
Wherever and in whatever manner there is a conjunction of substances, mantras, and ritual actions, [that is the means].
In each such case, in each such place, one should perform everything without omission.
Thus ends the subsequent method of instruction on Brahman through the six stages.
It has been declared as the most essential of the essential, being condensed yet possessing great significance.
The disciple.
Salutation to Śiva, who is accompanied by Umā, who is with the stars, and who is the sixfold self.
Salutations again and again to the one who is self-luminous, who shines by his own light, and who is independent.
He who practices this in such a manner is the all-pervading, supreme teacher.
The supreme state, the ultimate reality, as declared in the Parānubhava-sūtra. || 31 ||

[Thus ends the first section, titled "The Method for the Instruction on Brahman in Six Stages," in the dialogue between Guru and Disciple within the *Śrīśivasiddhāntatantra*, which elucidates the specific meanings.]
Salutations to the illustrious Nandikeśvara.
[In the second section: The Six-Stationed Worship of Brahman]
Now I shall describe in detail the procedure for the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
[It is performed] according to the ritual procedure for the presentation of offerings, distinguished by thirty-six varieties. || 1 ||
Worship is declared to be twelvefold by those devoted to the Shiva-siddhanta.
Likewise, the ritual services (upacāras) are recorded as being of twenty-four kinds. || 2 ||
The sprinkling with vibhūti upon the liṅga, as well as its consecration and bathing;
Likewise, there is the heating with charcoal and the fanning with incense.
Then follows the spreading of incense smoke and the adorning with fragrant garlands.
Likewise, the offering of unbroken grains and the presentation of flowers. || 4 ||
The lighting of the lamp and the offering of the food oblation.
The offering of betel-leaf and likewise the gifting of clothing;
Thus, the ritual for the worship of the Śiva-liṅga has been described in twelve ways.
The offering of a seat, the invitation, the arghya water, the water for washing the feet, and likewise the water for sipping;
And the sacred thread, garlands, ointments, and ornaments. || 6 ||
An umbrella, a fly-whisk, a palm-leaf fan, and a mirror.
The bell, the conch, song, instrumental music, dance, and circumambulation.
Salutation, praise, entreaty, and request, as well as dismissal;
Thus, these metaphorical designations (upacāras) are recorded as being of twenty-four kinds.
The application of the modes of worship and services is said to be thirty-sixfold.
"This state of Śiva consists of the thirty-six principles; such is the sacred tradition."
Now, the sequential method for the application of the offerings of worship is proclaimed.
Then, the purification through ash-baths and other rites should be performed according to the prescribed rules.
Then follows the practice of the illustrious five-syllabled mantra (Pañcākṣarī), and thereafter the ritual seat (āsana).
Then follows the supreme invocation in the form of the lotus-hand as a pedestal.
Having brought [the disciple], one should have him sit upon that seat, which is a liṅga situated on the limbs.
First, the sprinkling with the vibhūti, followed immediately by [the recitation] accompanied by mantras.
Then indeed, from the offering of the *arghya* up to the final sipping of water (*ācamana*), as well as the rite of bathing (*snāpana*).
The ten [practices], beginning with the heating by charcoal embers, are also stated as before. || 13 ||
Then, from the investiture with the sacred thread up to the final ritual instruction, it should be performed exactly as prescribed.
The dismissal consists of the re-establishment of the liṅga held in the hand back into its [own] body.
Thus, whoever performs the worship of the Liṅga with devotion, [attains the supreme goal].
By means of the prescribed ritual of service, he shall become one who knows how to offer everything to Śiva. || 15 ||
No absolute distinction between worship and offering is tenable.
The slight difference between these two is proclaimed on account of the distinction in their functions. || 16 ||
It depends upon worship and dedication for the purification of substances.
From the act of offering, the purification of the substance occurs, and immediately thereafter, grace [is bestowed].
By sprinkling with the *vibhūti*, the earth becomes completely purified within the *liṅga*.
Likewise, water [purifies] through bathing, and fire through the heating of charcoal.
Likewise, Vāyu [performed] the service of fanning with incense as directed by Śiva.
And by the smoke of incense, the sky [is adorned], and by the application of fragrant ornaments, the moon.
One should offer moonlight with camphor lamps and the stars with auspicious unbroken grains of rice.
Sūrya [is worshipped] with an offering of flowers, and Ātapa with a lamp of ghee. || 20 ||
The shadow [moves] behind, in front, and to the sides due to the movement of the lamp.
For cold, heat, and so forth indeed arise from those respective portions previously mentioned.
The Self is represented by the sacrificial offering, and the three qualities by the betel leaf.
Merely by putting on the garment, they are purified throughout the ten directions.
Thus, one should worship Śiva with acts of worship that depend upon such dedication;
having attained supreme purity of the ritual materials, one enjoys the bliss of His grace.
By the very bliss of his grace, one certainly becomes supreme. || 23 ||

The verse is as follows: Peace is the water, happiness is the *śama* (sandalwood paste), flowers are the auspicious mind, a lump of sandalwood is the unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), knowledge is the filaments, the flower is the Self itself, and fragrance shall be the incense.
The lamp, radiance, worship, great offerings of food (mahānaivedya), betel-leaf, and the essence of the nectar of one's own devotion— thus is the eightfold worship.
From here onwards, the specific sequence of Vīraśaiva worship shall be described.
I shall explain it in brief by way of its nature consisting of six stages.
Seated comfortably in a place of devotion, one should wear sacred ashes and rudrākṣa beads.
Having performed this with devotion, one whose self is thoroughly purified should then proceed to the site of Maheśvara.
Having practiced the supreme six-syllabled mantra with steadfast devotion to the Self.
Having taken the sacred site of Prasādi, he placed the Liṅga in his hand with great care.
Having performed worship at the site of Prāṇaliṅgin according to one's own experience, [one attains the goal].
Then, having offered it unto Śiva, he remained in his own abode out of joy.
And having attained satisfaction from the enjoyment of grace in the state of oneness.
Thus, through the state of equal flavor (samarasībhāva) and by means of the yoga of the six-limbed station (ṣaḍaṅga-sthala-yoga), [the goal is attained].
This very sequence for the worship of Vīraśaiva is performed at all times. || 29 ||
The etymological explanation (nirukti) of Vīraśaiva, which consists of two parts, is now being stated.
In this context, the word *vi* has the sense of "option" (*vikalpa*), and the word *ra* has the sense of "devoid of" (*rahita*).
That which is free from conceptual construction is Śaiva; it is remembered as Vīraśaiva.
That which is the supreme state, non-dual and without conceptual construction, is indeed one alone.
That is called Vīraśaiva; it is not the other [type] which involves conceptual construction (savikalpaka). || 31 ||
Thus, in brief, has the procedure for the worship of the Śiva-liṅga been declared.
In this Śivānubhavasūtra, on the path of the Śivasiddhānta. || 32 ||
The disciple said:
Salutations to you, the embodiment of Brahman in its six stages, whose fame is auspicious.
To Śambhu, who is self-cognizable, who is the heart, and whose form is pure knowledge.
Salutations to the one whose singular nature consists of the sixfold self through the union of the Liṅga and the Aṅga.
To Brahman of the six stations, the reality attained through the yoga of devotion and knowledge. || 34 ||
And light, the face, the form, and bliss are the manifestations of the Self.
O Śambhu, clarity of mind is your characteristic; it is of six kinds.
[In] Vṛtta meter: Your glory is supreme light; moreover, the rudrākṣa is your face, and the auspicious five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara-mantra) is clearly your divine name.
O Lord of Umā, your liṅga is your form; the nectar of supreme bliss flows from your feet.
"This grace has come from you"—such is my faithful devotion that worships you. (36)
O Destroyer of Cities, some devotee perceives You as "this one, this one," while another, through the yoga of knowledge born of their own devotion, perceives You as the All.
Thus, due to self-delusion, one perceives even this entire [universe] as Śiva through the application of illusory knowledge; it is other than that [reality]. (37)
Through the knowledge of the yoga of Māyā, all this is seen as a certain Śiva.
Through the knowledge born of the yoga of devotion, Śiva alone is seen as Śiva and no other. || 38 ||
Any other thought would be the wood; the thought of Śiva would be the oblation.
Fire does not exist within the wood; likewise, the fire of knowledge is said to be so described. || 39 ||
The verse: Mental, vocal, and physical actions are the fuels for merit and demerit.
The oblations belonging to Śiva are always offered by me as a sacrifice into the fire of knowledge.
Fire does not exist anywhere without wood, nor is it ever kindled; likewise, it does not transform through oblations and *svāhā*-utterances, nor does it reach satisfaction.

O Destroyer of Cities, having cast into the fire of knowledge this merit produced by the three organs— preceded by the kindling of rising sacred grass— one indeed offers the oblation of Śaiva devotion with one's own fervor. (41)
That action which consists of theft, violence, devotion to others' wives, and so forth, is sin; that which is the opposite of this is otherwise.
That which is the unshackled path distinguished by devotion, ritual action, and conduct—that here is Śaivism. (42)
It is eternally skilled in the art of self-surrender, serene, consisting of devotion, immovable,
and established through one's own innate disposition.
The noble ones declare that Śaiva action is one that delights in untainted enjoyment, is free from "I" and "mine," and transcends both [worlds];
having cast below and above the two fuels of merit and demerit.
And the fire of consciousness, having arisen from churning, shall again burn away that very [impurity].
Just as fire born from wood consumes that very wood.
In the same way, knowledge arising from action shall utterly destroy that very action. || 45 ||
I am neither a householder, nor a forest-dweller, nor a student, nor an ascetic, nor even one who has transcended the stages of life;
how much less so all these artificial designations? All this is merely imputed.

I am one whose nature is ever-playful and restless in the experience of the Supreme Self— the sun of the vision of consciousness-bliss that is inwardly manifest and easily attained through the auspicious Śaiva path of true dharma.
May these active functions of my senses, though they have arisen, fall back into their respective places.
O Lord, may there never be, even for a moment or in the slightest degree, the audacity to cause injury to the essence of non-difference from You through the ritual of worshipping the Śivaliṅga.
In speaking, in moving, in looking, and in all activities such as the worship of you;
O Blessed One, even lassitude is a sufficient ornament for a devoted servant. (48)

You are the Self; Girijā is your intellect; your attendants are your vital breaths; your body is your home; the arrangement for enjoying sense objects is your worship; and sleep is your state of meditative absorption.
The movement of my feet, the rite of circumambulation, all songs of praise, and whatever action I perform—all that, O Śambhu, is your worship. (49)

O Supreme One, whose nature is the realization of the non-duality of the Self and the Lord—though You are the very limb of devotion—I beg of You this one boon; for indeed, there is nothing whatsoever that is impossible for You.
O Father, may you be well-pleased with the affectionate love for the childhood of your own son, during which I played together with my body, senses, and their objects as my companions. (50)
The master is independent; the non-master is not independent. Whatever the master desires, that I do.
Indeed, by his own will, he is neither the doer nor the master nor the independent agent of both merit and demerit for the two [the self and the body]. (51)
He who possesses the triad of powers—will, knowledge, and action—is the Lord.
"O Independent One, this one is dependent on you; I am not independent, for I am without power. (52)
The meter is Vṛtta.
It desires, it knows, and it performs all this—both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
Through the power of will, knowledge, and action, Śiva alone exists; "I am not" is the truth. || 53 ||
Only one who possesses power can be capable; one who lacks power would be incapable.
One who is capable accomplishes everything; what can one who is incapable do? || 54 ||
In verse: By the power of will you become the Lord; by the power of knowledge, O Śambhu, you know everything that is known; and endowed with the power of action, you perform all deeds.

You are the agent of all actions performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, and you are the enjoyer of their fruit; yet through your sovereignty and lordship, you laugh, for while you are untainted, I am tainted. || 55 ||
Impelled by you, I perform all actions; I am not the doer, nor am I the enjoyer of their fruit, because of my state of dependence.
O Lord of Umā, just as a punishment for a servant's offense would fall upon his master, so too has that very same thing been done by me unto you.
O Śambhu, if I were independent, I would indeed have no fear at all.
I perform meritorious and sinful deeds, and I withdraw them through my own divine play.
Therefore, O Lord, having understood this from both the perspective of dependence and independence, [I have come to you].
"It is the truth that there is not even the slightest thing such as merit or sin. (58)
Therefore, both merit and demerit, as well as heaven and the miserable states of existence, [arise from this].
Both bondage and liberation belong to you alone, O Lord, and not to me.
He who in the past determined, "This is merit" and "This is evil."
In the absence of those two, who is that agent? Let it be said: "I am he. (60)
But the distinction between day and night is indeed like that of one born blind.
Even my discrimination between merit and demerit is not as [clear] for me, who am ignorant of my birth. (61)
This state of dependence has been offered by me with devotion at the feet of the Guru.
By the power of His grace, there remains the realization: "I am not anyone at all."
The meter is Vṛtta.
Only Someśvara knows my welfare in this world and the next, not I myself.
I know everything, yet I possess no inherent capacity for knowing that belongs to the Lord.
He who practices this in such a manner is the all-pervading and most excellent teacher.
The supreme state, the ultimate truth, as declared in the Parānubhava-sūtra. || 64 ||

[Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of the Śiva-liṅga," in the dialogue between Guru and Disciple within the *Śrīśivasiddhāntatantra*, which elucidates the specific meanings.]
Salutations to the venerable Guru Basava Liṅga.
[The Existence of Grace in the Third Section:
Now, in this Anubhava-sūtra, that which was previously uttered from the mouth of Śiva—
I shall now describe the true nature of the glorious grace.
This is the determination of the principles concerning the three: the world, the individual soul, and the Lord.
The three [types of] gifts of food from remnants are determined in their proper sequence. || 2 ||
The world-form consisting of the body and so forth is a remnant characterized by delusion.
Food is that [element], and the individual soul (jīva), characterized by worldly existence, would be its presiding deity. || 3 ||
The Lord Prasāda is manifestly characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Having thus stated its essential nature, the specific details are now further explained.
He sees that body, yet he does not see that [self-]body.
Another person sees those two, yet they both do not see him. || 5 ||
Thus, having taken as his subject matter the supreme meaning, both external and internal.
The divine devotion consists in the unity of both knowledge and action.
The disciple said:
To the one whose essential nature is ineffable, who bestows the state of Śiva.
Salutations to the true Guru, the Lord, who is the embodiment of Brahman in its six aspects.
The meter is Vṛtta.
To the Guru, the greatly compassionate one, who is serene and established in his own state of the sixfold Brahman;
Then, having bowed with supreme devotion, the disciple, with palms joined in reverence and speech restrained, asked:
"O Guru, O treasure-house of the knowledge of Śiva, O soul of Śiva, regarding these determinations of the six stations (ṣaṭsthala) spoken by you..."
Out of compassion, I have understood something; may you grant me favor regarding what I have reflected upon therein.
Furthermore, some say that food kept in a vessel is what is offered as a prasāda to Śiva.
"Since that which was consumed by you, O Lord, is indeed nothing but leavings, tell me the truth:
how did this rice become a divine favor from the very beginning?"
O true guru, tell me at the end how this remains as leavings; explain its ultimate meaning to me.
O Lord, how is it that a single reality is divided into these three?
Among those three, what is to be accepted? Tell me the reason for that.
The meter is Vṛtta.
Thus questioned, he who possesses the majesty of unsurpassed bliss remained silent.
Having gazed upon himself for a long time as self-luminous, the Lord Guru spoke to his disciple.
The Guru.
"O child, you have asked what has never been asked by anyone before—this wonder that is higher than the highest."
I shall explain the nature of grace as a distinct category; listen attentively for a moment, and do not consider it to be a mere remnant of something else.
Grace is devoid of beginning and end; it is itself of an indivisible nature, characterized by its own remaining essence.
"Free from conceptual construction, it is the perfectly pure reality"—this is its power, arising from its own innate nature. || 15 ||
The disciple said: [In verse:]
O Lord, what was said by you to me previously? You described the Liṅga as being without beginning or end.
Free from conceptual construction and remaining as that which is left over, this is the indivisible form, perfectly pure. || 16 ||
The Guru.
Listen, my child, you whose intellect has accomplished its purpose; these words of mine, though seemingly replete with censure, shine forth as being endowed with true meaning.
I tell you: there is no difference at all between the state of being subsumed and the clarity of the characteristic. || 17 ||
That in which substances such as food dissolve, and that from which they are derived.
That linga exists as grace, and for that very reason, it is grace itself.
Either by way of worshiping the gateway or by way of offering the linga oneself.
This single state is designated by the term "serenity" (prasāda) through the lens of devotion. || 19 ||
The disciple.
The true nature of grace has been understood by me through the characteristics already described.
O true Guru, please tell me out of compassion: what is the nature of the categories of existence?
The Guru. The meter.
An entity brings about clarity for an object, and again brings about clarity at the time of its application.
The disciple [says]: "It spreads forth for a moment the meaning of the word in the middle, which is immeasurable in its beginning and end, as a state of serene clarity. (21)
O Lord, when you were asked by me here, "What is the nature of an object?", why was this said to me?
Since it is said that "only grace is bestowed as the object [of attainment]," the failure of grace has been described. || 22 ||
The Guru.
Listen, O child of noble mind; I shall speak to you of the ultimate truth.
The non-failure of faith and the failure of that which is imagined. || 23 ||
The meter.
Just as gold fashioned into a necklace is not destroyed by its transformation into that form, so too it does not cease to exist in its nature as gold.
Likewise, understand that even this grace, though imagined for the sake of the object, exists by virtue of the thought "it is myself. (24)
A golden image is pleasing because of its quality of being a beautiful ornament.
In whatever manner this grace has been described as a distinct entity, [it remains so]. 25.
The meter is Vṛtta.
For the purpose of awakening the existence of faith, by means of various services consisting of ritual actions.
The state of being the surrenderer effortlessly extends even to the meaning of the word "grace. || 26 ||
The disciple: [This is] the meter.
The nature of an object is known to be conceptualized, and its destruction is also conceptualized because it too is conceptualized.
What is said to be "bhāva," and what is this "viniyoga"? Therefore, please tell me out of compassion. || 27 ||
The Guru.
This true state of serenity has been rightly inquired about by the Great-souled One.
I shall explain it in brief; listen with a concentrated mind. || 28 ||
Devotion, which has Śiva alone as its object, is itself here described as the very state of being.
Viniyoga is the form of action, characterized by the worship of Śiva and so forth. || 29 ||
The disciple.
O best of teachers, what is this that you have said here—this application of such an intrinsic nature?
I have indeed asked about this devotion; you have mentioned the ritual—let it be explained to me.
The Glorious Guru.
Indeed, this discernment of yours is excellent, for it indicates both great fortune and the meaning of what follows.
In this context, devotion consists of action; that very state of being, when joined with application, is devotion.
The disciple.
By your grace, I have come to understand devotion consisting of action.
"O Lord, best among the knowers of reality, tell me: what is the nature of action? (32)
The Guru.
Whatever action there is, whether external or internal, born of mind, speech, or body;
It is considered to consist of taking up, offering, worshiping, recitation, and meditation. || 33 ||
The disciple.
O best of gurus, when I asked, "What is the nature of action?"—
What did you say regarding taking, giving, and so forth? Let that be told.
The venerable Guru.
And it is proclaimed that "taking" (ādāna) means receiving the grace of Śiva.
The offering is the presentation of an object; this is its dedication to Śiva. || 35 ||
Worship of Śiva is pūjā; the recollection of Śiva-mantras is japa.
The very contemplation of the nature of Śiva is designated as meditation (dhyāna). || 36 ||
The disciple. [The verse is finished.]
The true nature of action has been understood by me through your compassionate glance directed toward its detailed exposition.
O All-pervading Lord, as before, You have clearly explained this essential nature of the primordial devotion.
The illustrious Guru. Metre.
Listen, my child, to something of the true nature of devotion; even Śiva is not capable of describing it fully.
"What wonder can there be that Śambhu was unable here to fulfill this rite of devotion? (38)
Devotion is independent, having brought the Lord under its own control; it is innate, with the singular majesty of self-experience.

The self-originated devotion, following the path of its own scripture, acting according to its own will, shining with its own delight, distinguished, manifold, intent on ritual action, consisting of knowledge, and removing the delusion of the universe, reigns supreme.
The pure Viśvāsinī, renowned as a follower of the heroic Śambhu, shines forth as a ground of rest. || 40 ||
Devotion is desireless, supreme destiny, free from illusion, and resting upon the partless and actionless.
Free from doubt, unwavering, unrestrained, and beyond reproach, the intellect of certain conviction shines forth. || 41 ||
Devotion, hidden yet consisting of one's own essential nature, bestows the abode of the bliss of supreme liberation.
Bodiless, objectless, devoid of senses, and absolute, she shines as the eternal state.
Devotion, which has cast aside all the defects of evil speech, is difficult for those of wicked conduct and ill fortune to attain.

Devotion, which removes suffering, performs what is difficult to accomplish, and is auspicious, shines forth with qualities that are hard to understand and difficult to cross over; it is ever-arisen, endowed with right conduct, possessed of virtuous latent impressions, and has the true bliss of the Self as its very form. || 43 ||
Being characterized by the radiance of existence, she shines forth as consisting of being and consciousness, and as possessing virtuous conduct.
Devotion that is serene and free from pride bestows the vision of direct perception and the realization of the truth.

Time does not possess the vital breath as its mark, nor do those possessing the vital breath possess the mark of time.
Action also, through conventional usage, is attributed to time. || 58 ||
That which is to be performed as appropriate for the occasion is proclaimed as "karma" (action).
Without the ripening of the karma of time, there is nothing at all that exists.
When the vital breath becomes separated from the body at the time of death, [one should recite this mantra].
Then, indeed, there is a separation between those two, the external body and the linga. || 60 ||
What difference is there here in separation between those two who are devoid of knowledge?
When union is perceived, separation is its opposite.
Since the vital self (prāṇātman), which understands both separation and union, has departed from there.
Through investigation, [it is established] for the purpose of negating the identity of the liṅga and the body, and also for the purpose of establishing the injunction.
In reality, there is no gender-sign of the body either at the beginning or at the end.
Having come together once more in the midst, he departed again; tell me, what wonder is there in this? || 63 ||
At the outset, the wearing of the topknot and the sacred thread is prescribed according to the ritual injunctions.
The abandonment of that topknot and sacred thread at the end is recommended in whatever manner [is appropriate]. || 64 ||
Therefore, it is not contradictory for the separation of the subtle body (liṅga) and the physical body (aṅga) to occur at the end.
And it does not lead to fault even in subsequent actions that ought to be performed.
Having cast off the body at the end, that self consisting of vital breath indeed entered [into it].
Therefore, he himself becomes separated from that body of the liṅga within his own chosen liṅga.
Having surrendered his own life-breaths, he remains concentrated upon his own chosen *liṅga*.
Remaining well-concealed, he is then separated from that subtle body (liṅgadeha).
For it is the body alone that is fit for consecration at the end, according to the prescribed rule.
Therefore, this [ordinary] linga is not suitable; one should worship having taken up [the true] linga. || 68 ||
One of pure intellect [should worship] the Self of Śiva residing in the liṅga, together with the liṅga.
Having taken it up and placed it himself upon a pedestal, he should worship it day after day.
Or one should always wear the linga established together with the Guru.
For one whose self is Śiva, there is no depositing of a deposit in a Śiva-liṅga.
There is not even burning for one who is merged in the self-luminous Linga, much less anything else.
Just as the Self residing within the body cannot be burned or destroyed, so too [is it].
"Likewise, 'the Self abiding in the liṅga'—this is the established position of those who know reality. (71)
This is indeed ungraspable, unburnable, undissoluble, and also undrying.
This [Self] is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient.
For one whose body has already been cast off, there is neither concealment nor cremation.
Therefore, the *liṅga* is to be accepted, while the body is to be abandoned by its very nature.
For the Veda declares: "Having indeed cast off the body, one attains union with Śiva. (73)
In reality, it consists of the wick, the base of the lamp, and the tip of the flame.
An illustration is seen in the world regarding the state of the oneness of the individual soul and the Lord.
The body is the wick, the life-force is the base of the lamp, and the Lord is the flame of the lamp.
The three [types] are declared to be rājasa, tāmasa, and sāttvika, respectively.
For the body is indeed inert; the living soul would thus be designated as both inert and non-inert.
The Supreme Lord is non-inert; their unity exists only in the absence of anything inert.
There is no difference [between them], just as there is none between the base and the tip of a lamp when its wick is extinguished.
Indeed, there is no difference between the individual soul and the Lord even at the time of casting off the body.
A devotee should not cast the linga upon the ground together with his body.
If one should cast it down through delusion, it will certainly lead to fault. || 78 ||
Nevertheless, that which is joined among the joined is yet dissociated from actions among actions.
Therefore, for one who is endowed with the limbs of the *liṅga* and possesses the splendor of Brahman in its six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*), [there is liberation]. || 79 ||
One should not perform funeral rites for him here on earth, as one would for domestic animals.
There is no corpse for him, because [otherwise] impurities such as birth-impurity (sūtaka) would attach to him. || 80 ||
Impurity would not apply at all, especially in the case of his sons and others.
If impurity lasts for only a moment, even that flees from bathing.
Nor are rites such as the *śrāddha* performed, nor the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), nor the water-libation ceremony (*udakakriyā*).
One should not perform the Pārvaṇa and other rites for a yogin who has become one with Śiva.
Now, if one also desires to perform a ritual action directed toward this [deity], [the following should be done].
One should perform only what is auspicious and satisfy those who are devoted to Śiva. || 83 ||
And every year, he should feed devotees of Śiva in honor of him.
For food given to devotees is indeed as good as given to Śiva himself.
One should behave toward the wife of the guru and his sons as one does toward the guru himself. || 84 ||
The disciple: [The] meter.

May my body, along with its vital breaths, become hidden through constant contemplation and remembrance of the feet of the Guru— the one who possesses the fullness of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*) of the Guru’s state, who is endowed with the qualities of the specific name bestowed by the true Śambhu-like Sadguru, who is the supreme bliss of the dense mass of true consciousness at the feet of the Guru, and who is gracious through the excellence of that supreme Self. 85.

The Liṅga, situated within the direct perception [of the yogi], slowly, slowly, and uniformly from all sides, manifests its own most intense power of radiance, like the moon and fire, for one to behold.
O Śambhu, at the conclusion of my *prārabdha* karma, may You, assuming the form of a pillar of light, graciously accept this body of mine; O Most Compassionate One, I beg for this boon of mine. (86)
O Śambhu, may I, together with my body, abide in this supremely radiant *liṅga* of yours.
Grant me this boon: that at the time of my death, you may generally remain with me through your compassion so that I may be absorbed [in you]. (87)
While the self-luminous mark of the Supreme Self resides within the palm of my hand, this body of mine [is but a mere vessel].
It would remain hidden here within this cause of manifold variety, like a piece of gold within the womb of the fire.
The body is said to be the region of the palms, and the individual soul (jīva) is the region of the eyes.
The junction between the body and the life-force is designated as the *liṅga*. || 89 ||
In this [liṅga], the body of Śiva is pure and fragrant with camphor, and it takes the form of a lamp whose innate radiance is established as most excellent.

May both these forms of mine, through the yoga of my own devotion, finally dissolve into the state of the Great Guru (Mahāguru). And regarding these three—the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) and the others—residing in the abode of grace for his devotees, who bear the marks of the earth, the fire, the digit of the moon, and the sky; in them, we pray with the deepest intensity.
The grace of compassion. || 91 ||
The transformation of the stage of the devotee is the stage of Maheśvara; likewise, it is the stage of Ubha.
The transformation of the state of grace and refuge is the unification with the *prāṇaliṅga*. || 92 ||
The Guru is the state of transformation into the Ācāra-liṅga, while the Cāra is the state of transformation into the liṅga known as Śaiva.
"The state of transformation into the Liṅga of the temple shall indeed be great"; thus did the Veda proclaim these six sacred sites. || 93 ||
Having offered these three types of limbs (aṅgas) to the triad of liṅgas—the Ācāra-liṅga, the Śiva-liṅga, and the Mahāprasāda-liṅga—[one attains the goal].
They have attained the supreme state that transcends both the sign (liṅga) and the embodied soul (aṅgin); I choose this supreme grace born of compassion. || 94 ||
The earthly body is the bull, while the fiery body is the king of tawny bulls.
The Vaiyyataka, the Ālāma, and the Vibhu—thus the classification of their bodies has been taught. || 95 ||

The differentiation of qualities in earth, water, fire, air, and space is said to proceed according to a gradual sequence; then, externally, there is the specific form of the Liṅga, while internally, there is the supreme form.

The essence of the Sūtra remains non-conceptual, free from the distinctions of the qualities (guṇas), itself devoid of sequential gradations among these [states], possessing both form and space. || 96 ||
The subtle forms [of the elements] appear in sequence as a lump of clay, a cloud, a stone, a spark, a whirlwind, and a rainbow.
There may be those called earthen, watery, and fiery, as well as those distinguished by the divisions of wind and space, known as the airy and the ethereal. || 97 ||
Thus, the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) would possess the characteristic of supreme liberation.
Purified by that very state of being, his conduct is directly sanctifying.
Through the experience of grace obtained by means of the unsurpassed compassion of these three— the Guru, the Lord’s feet, and the form of Śiva—
I have thus declared this supreme and most secret treasure, which is endowed with the meaning of the profound dialogue between the venerable Teacher and his foremost disciple. 99.
The feet of the Guru remove fear; they are the ornament for the heart seeking refuge and the source of one's own bliss.
I praise that which provides deliverance from the fear of death, and which acts as a veil against the rays of the young dawn.
Grant me supreme devotion alone, steadfast in Your feet.
O Someśvara, embodiment of compassion, I desire nothing other than this. || 101 ||
Just as that which is unknown remains unknown, so too everything remains known within [the interval].
O Lord of Umā, in that same way, everything else would remain unknown to me.
O Lord, I do not know what is beneficial or what is harmful, nor anything else whatsoever.
You alone know all that; do for me whatever is beneficial.
This alone is our boon; this very thing we choose.
"O Lord Someśvara, instruct me on this very same matter constantly. (104)
O abode of compassion, O delight in compassion, O mine of compassion, O ocean of compassion!
O ocean of compassion, O impeller of mercy, O ornament of compassion, protect me! 104.
O Lord, you who grant the taste of knowledge that severs the bonds of saṃsāra!
O glorious Someśa of Aipura, salutations to you, whose self consists of the six stations (ṣaṭsthalātman). || 105 ||
Thus, this [work], consisting of the two parts—the preceding and the succeeding—has been declared and established.
Herein is completed the *Śivasiddhāntatantra*, the *Śivānubhavasūtra*. 106.
He who practices this in such a manner is the all-pervading one, the most excellent teacher.
The supreme state, the ultimate truth, as declared in the Parānubhava-sūtra. || 107 ||

[Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Conclusion of the Body," in the Śivasiddhāntatantra composed by the illustrious Māyideva, which elucidates the specific meanings within the dialogue between teacher and disciple.]
